title: Nakamura Declares Bullet Brawl A "Marathon, Not A Sprint" After 71st Victory
summary: GM Hikaru Nakamura extended the most dominant run in Bullet Brawl history on Saturday, cruising to a resounding 46-point victory with a score of 190 points. The American secured his sixth consecutive first-place finish and netted the $400 first prize on the back of consistent play. GMs Jose Martinez, Faustino Oro, and IM Reza Mahdavi followed, however Nakamura spent more of the tournament focused on reaching a score of 200 points rather than worrying about his pursuers. While Nakamura forged ahead, FM Anastasia Avramidou picked up the best women's prize after a tight race with WIM Melika Mohammadi. The next edition of Bullet Brawl will begin on Saturday, October 24, at 12 p.m. ET / 18:00 CEST / 9:30 p.m. IST. Standings

title: Bodhana & Co. Test Favorites As European Club Cup Begins In Budva
summary: The top teams could rest the likes of GMs Nodirbek Abdusattorov, Anish Giri, and Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus while still scoring 6-0 clean sweeps in round one of the 41st European Chess Club Cup in Budva, Montenegro. GM Nils Grandelius was one of the few stars to fall, to 55-year-old Serbian CM Slobodan Filipovic, but the Swedish number-one's team Novy Bor Chess Club still won 5-1. On paper, the story was similar in the 30th European Women's Chess Club Cup, but the 3.5-0.5 victory for defending champion Cercle d'Echecs de Monte-Carlo over the young English team of She Plays To Win Lionesses A was incredibly hard-fought. WFM Anusha Subramanian held chess legend GM Pia Cramling to a draw, while the top-rated women's player in the event, GM Aleksandra Goryachkina, only overcame 11-year-old WGM-elect Bodhana Sivanandan in 77 moves. Round two is on Sunday, October 18, starting at 8 a.m. ET / 14:00 CEST / 5:30 p.m. IST. The European Chess Club Cup was first held in 1956 in Belgrade, Yugoslavia (now Serbia), and has been a regular event since 1976, an annual event since 1992, and saw the inclusion of a women's tournament from 1996 onward. It's a seven-round Swiss team event, with six players per team (plus two reserves) in the Open, and four players (plus one reserve) in the Women's. The short format, running Saturday, October 17, to Friday, October 23, means it's a sprint, with GM David Navara saying after his round-one win: "Of course, it's not easy here, because there are many teams, and with seven rounds it’s a bit random—which can be both good and bad for us—so we will see!" With seven rounds it's a bit random—which can be both good and bad for us—so we will see! —David Navara (Novy Bor Chess Club) Many teams is no exaggeration, since there are as many as 107 in the Open and 22 in the Women's, with players ranging from the world elite to regular club players—with commentator GM Simon Williams noting that both local bars near the venue ran out of beer on the eve of the tournament. There's €40,000 in prize money at stake for the top teams, however, who have gathered together some of the world's best players. Defending champion SuperChess Romania was led by GM Gukesh Dommaraju in 2025, but this year features the world number-five—Olympiad star and newly-engaged Abdusattorov! Congratulations to Nodirbek Abdusattorov and Sevinch Mavlonova on their engagement! ❤️ Erdogmus, the highest-rated 15-year-old of all time, will be another player to watch, and his Turkish team of Bayegan Pendik Chess Sports Club, which also features Giri, GM Amin Tabatabaei, and GM Richard Rapport, is the top seed for a second year in a row (in 2024 they had to settle for fourth place). Second-seeded Alkaloid is topped by GMs Wei Yi and Arjun Erigaisi, who both played in round one. The stakes are higher this year, since the top four teams will qualify for a new eight-team event, the €300,000 European Chess Super League to be held in Bucharest, Romania on February 2-10, 2027. With the recent sponsorship agreements signed, ECU is almost doubling its budget for 2027 and launching an elite event, the European Chess Super League, with the participation of traditional clubs in Europe and beyond. The European Chess Super League is based on competitive criteria, as at least five clubs will qualify from the European Club Cup 2026 in Budva, Montenegro. #EliteChess #clubs #sports #bucharestt #superfoundation The women's lineup in Budva is also strong, with three 2500+ players, including women's number-five Goryachkina, number-nine GM Koneru Humpy, and number-10 IM Polina Shuvalova. The Swiss format means the favorites get opposition they're expected to dominate in round one, and that's largely what happened. There was predictable carnage in the top-three matches, with all the favorites winning 6-0. There were many stories along the way, however, including 59-year-old FM Dave Ledger, one of three Ledger brothers on the Blackthorne team, playing, on GM Williams' recommendation, the Kilkenny Gambit with 1.d4 Nf6 2.g4?! against 17-year-old GM Ediz Gurel. He even played it with GM Shakhriyar Mamedyarov, a player synonymous with early g4s, sitting next to him. Dave Ledger hits Ediz Gurel with the Kilkenny Gambit! https://t.co/zSZqAnNmIa https://t.co/wo3liSzB4y The Turkish youngster commented: "I knew my opponent was an aggressive player, I saw some of his games. I wasn’t expecting something this aggressive on move two, but it was an interesting game!" Perhaps inevitably, Black won swiftly, but getting a grandmaster opponent to think for almost seven minutes after move two is also an achievement!

title: So Sole Leader After Turnaround Win; Li And Lee Lead Women's
summary: GM Wesley So remained the only unbeaten player and sole leader of the 2026 U.S. Chess Championship with five points when he fought back from a worse position to defeat GM Ray Robson in round seven. Among the joint leaders from the previous round, GMs Fabiano Caruana and Andy Woodward drew their respective games to follow the leader on 4.5 points, while GM Awonder Liang crashed to defeat in just 27 moves against GM Grigoriy Oparin with uncharacteristic tactical oversights. The 2026 U.S. Women's Chess Championship saw WIM Rachael Li and IM Alice Lee emerge as joint leaders on 5.5 points after confident victories. The other joint leader and the only undefeated player of the event till now, WGM Thalia Cervantes, overextended her position and lost to IM Anna Sargsyan while trying to win. GM Irina Krush won a topsy-turvy game against IM Carissa Yip and jumped into sole second with five points. The round once again produced five decisive games. Looking at some of the tactical mistakes from both tournaments, fatigue seems to be a major factor, as the tournament approaches its final leg. Round eight is on Saturday, October 17, starting at 1 p.m. ET / 19:00 CEST / 10:30 p.m. IST. Standings After Round 7: Open Standings After Round 7: Women Round 7 Results: Open Even though there were four players at the top after the sixth round, we had interesting predictions at the beginning of the games. Obviously, the system is stacked in favor of rating favorites and ex-champions, with Caruana and So being the top two seeds as well as having won the title five and three times before, respectively. It was a difficult day for one of the leaders, Liang, who seemed to be quite off-color. His decision to close the center with 17...c5 was puzzling, effectively rendering his own dark-squared bishop distinctly ineffective for the rest of the game. His subsequent mistakes indicate fatigue, as the final tactic was definitely not a hard one to foresee for a player of his caliber.

title: Olympiad qualification spots for 2027 World Cup and Women’s World Cup announced
summary: FIDE announces the allocation of qualification spots for the 2027 FIDE World Cup and Women’s World Cup, based on the results of the Chess Olympiad held in Samarkand, Uzbekistan. FIDE is pleased to announce the allocation of qualification spots for the 2027 FIDE World Cup and Women’s World Cup, based on the results of the Chess Olympiad held in Samarkand, Uzbekistan. These prestigious tournaments will showcase top players who have earned their places through exceptional performances at the Olympiad, alongside those who qualify via other pathways. Spot transfers to continental events FIDE World Cup and Women’s World Cup regulations allow each continent to transfer allocated Olympiad spots to their respective continental events. This provision grants continental federations greater flexibility in offering World Cup qualification through local competitions. Prior to the Olympiad, the federations of Europe, Africa, and the Americas chose to exercise this option, transferring a portion of their Olympiad-earned spots to upcoming continental tournaments. This adjustment provides additional opportunities for players to qualify regionally and encourages stronger competition at the continental level. Olympiad spots transferred to Continental Events in accordance with decisions of Continental federations Final Olympiad qualification spots After transferring 17 open and 5 women’s Olympiad spots, as indicated above, 83 national federations from the Open section and 45 federations from the Women’s section have secured places in the 2027 World Cup and Women’s World Cup, respectively. These Olympiad-based slots are awarded to the top-performing national teams, ensuring that the highest-level performers from the Olympiad will compete on chess’s biggest stage. title: My 70th Memorable Game
summary:
On 17th October 1956, a sensational sacrificial game played in New York City by a 13-year-old chess upstart from Brooklyn shot across the globe. It was a game that literally took the chess world by storm. It contains a stunning sacrificial onslaught and is regarded as one of the most famous games of chess that has ever been played. In the October issue of CHESS magazine John Henderson recalls the game that made 13-year-old Bobby Fischer famous. It was played seventy years ago, today.

The upstart in question is, of course, Robert James ‘Bobby’ Fischer, and the sheer brilliance of his victory over the highly-experienced Donald Byrne, at the third Lessing J. Rosenwald Trophy, led to the game being billed by Hans Kmoch as the “Game of the Century” in the December 1956 issue of Chess Review and the title stuck. (Though in a misprint, it appeared alongside a front-cover picture of a young Fischer, but when you went, as instructed, to page 370 the game in question turned out to be the equally impressive Smyslov-Pachman from the 1956 Moscow Olympiad.)

It was indeed a breathtaking game that proved to be Fischer’s calling card as a potential world champion-in-the-making. And such was its impact, the game even featured prominently in leading Soviet chess magazines of the day, as the Russians started to compile a ‘Fischer file’. Before this game, Fischer was untitled and little-known outside of New York, let alone the US. However, after the game, everyone knew who he was, because just a little more than two years later, he was playing in the Candidates, the world’s youngest grandmaster, and seriously talked up as being a future world title contender.

So this game was the first blow of his trumpet. Donald Byrne (the younger and more affable of the famous Byrne playing brothers; the eldest, Robert, going on to become a grandmaster and also a world title Candidate), was a very strong amateur and a professor at Penn State University, who gained the IM title and had won the 1953 US Open – but even he never saw the true depth of Fischer’s stunning sacrificial assault, believing right up to the very moment of truth with 17...Be6!! that he stood better.

Surprisingly, in 1969, Fischer didn’t include this historic game in his must-read all-time classic anthology, My 60 Memorable Games, but this was so typically systematic of Fischer. His rationale was that he’d already published it with light annotations in his earlier 1959 book, Bobby Fischer’s Games of Chess, which contained 34 of his early games up to 1958, and despite how commercially popular his Byrne brilliancy would be with deeper notes, he didn’t see the appeal, nor the need, to reproduce it again.

From my own personal perspective, my first time seeing this game came not long after learning to play, caught up in the media swirl of the Fischer-Spassky world championship match, so circa late October 1972, following yet another trip to my local William Patrick Memorial Library in Kirkintilloch. There I found to my delight on the Reykjavik-inspired bulging chess section shelf, a copy of the 1970 tome from publishers George Bell & Sons, The King-Hunt by W H Cozens (with its distinctive light-blue dust jacket), where it appears as game 38 in the author’s 45-game anthology devoted to the pursuit and tracking down of the king.

If we step back in time to 70 years ago, things were beginning to click at the chessboard for the young Bobby Fischer. He’d emerged from his much-vaunted 11-year-old “I just got good” days of 1954, and with each tournament and game throughout 1956, he was rapidly improving. Curiously, he started the year as something of a gifted amateur, but by the end of it, he was a solid master firmly on a trajectory to stardom. In an email exchange, chess author, historian and Fischer maven IM John Donaldson (whose latest book on his chess hero is the very readable Inside the Mind of Bobby Fischer) attributes this, in part, to his total immersion in the game when he enrolled in Jack Collins’ self-styled “crucible of chess genius”, the Hawthorne Chess Club, in the June of 1956.

The results thereafter were impressive. Fischer appeared for the first time on the cover of a chess magazine, as the 13-year-old won his first US title by dominating the 11th US Junior Championship held at the Franklin Chess Club in Philadelphia. Chess Life, the magazine of the United States Chess Federation, celebrated his achievement with a cover story in its 20th July 1956 issue. Little were they to know that this was just the start of a roller-coaster ride that would usher in the Fischer era.

The Montreal Star was quick to spot Fischer’s potential when the 13 year old arrived in their city to take part in the Canadian Open, where he was far from disgraced finishing joint eighth.

Fischer’s junior triumph was followed by a heightened summer of chess activity with barely a break, starting first with the US Open Championship in Oklahoma City from 17th to 28th July. There, without a loss, he scored 8½-3½ to finish tied for fourth to eighth places. At the conclusion of the tournament, Tony Saidy’s family hosted Bobby on Martha’s Vineyard for a short break and it was while there that he received a personal invitation to play in his very first ‘overseas’ tournament, the Canadian Open, in Montreal, 25th August to 2nd September, where he stayed with William Hornung, the tournament director. Interviewed by The Montreal Star about his young house guest’s non-stop passion for chess, morning, noon and night, Hornung commented: “That boy! He even plays expert chess while he’s sleeping.”

In the Canadian Open, Fischer finished in eighth to twelfth places, only one point behind joint winners and top seeds Larry Evans and William Lombardy. After the event, Bobby then got a ride back to NYC from Evans, who later wrote that during the six-hour drive home he talked non-stop about chess, and nothing but chess, even to the extent of ignoring Evans’ wife.

After the Canadian Open, the next stop was the tournament that made Fischer’s name. In the autumn of 1956 (7th-24th October), he was allowed time off school to play in the annual Rosenwald Trophy Memorial – an invitational tournament held at the famous Marshall Chess Club and for this edition, expanded to twelve top players from the USA to allow the Brooklyn schoolboy, as the newly-crowned US Junior Champion, to compete. Fischer’s final result of 4½/11 (eighth-to-tenth place) was not exactly spectacular, but what was truly spectacular was his round 8 game against Donald Byrne, the ‘Game of the Century’. And from that very moment, the face of American chess was to dramatically change, as the game shot across the world.

This was the game 70 years ago that subsequently appeared in every newspaper chess column and chess magazine. How did our own Chess Magazine cover Fischer’s 1956 brilliancy? Well…we didn’t! For some inexplicable reason, it didn’t appear. To our horror, all we could find in our archives was a one paragraph snippet of news under the headline “New York’s New Chess Prodigy” that appeared in the November 9, 1956 issue (Nos. 279-80, p.35) of Chess. It reported that Sammy Reshevsky had won the 3rd Rosenwald tournament, a prestigious event which was marked by a controversial double default and a remarkable game: “Donald Byrne was beaten by a thirteen-year old boy named Fischer (who totalled 4½ points) in a game of great depth and brilliancy, which we shall publish later.”

Despite an exhaustive search (from our editorial team, John Saunders, and even Canadian-based chess author, collector, and historian Alan McGowan), we couldn’t find the game appearing in any of the magazine indexes from 1956 through to the end of 1959. Just in case, we even searched through all of Leonard Barden’s wonderfully instructive and entertaining ‘How Good Is Your Chess?’ columns during this period, lest it had been slipped in there. A good try – but, alas, still no joy.

We can only assume this rather strange omission was down to some really bad timing for Baruch H. Wood, the magazine’s legendary founding editor. The appearance of Fischer’s “Game of the Century” would have hit the chess scene during a very busy period for the magazine: BH was frantically finishing off his mega report with many games from the 1956 Moscow Olympiad, after which came the Christmas edition of the magazine (always a headache), followed by the extremely popular Hastings report, which, back then, was one of the world’s top elite events. That particular edition was jointly won by Svetozar Gligoric and a young Bent Larsen, in what was the Dane’s debut appearance, and would have appeared in the late January/February 1957 (and probably even stretching through to March) editions of the magazine. We’re sure the game did eventually appear in the magazine at some later date during the 1960s/70s – but it certainly didn’t appear, as promised, in the final few years of the 1950s. So, as an atonement of sorts, we bring you the game in this, its 70th anniversary month. And no matter how many times I’ve seen this game, it never fails to enthrall me – and hopefully it will similarly enlighten and captivate a generation of younger players who are new to the game and perhaps not aware of this amazing Fischer brilliancy.

And it comes with a big bonus for our readers, with many thanks to American collector and historian David DeLucia, who has built an incredible library of chess books, manuscripts, documents and ephemera that’s unlike any other collection in the world, either publicly or privately.

David is also a passionate collector of all odd sorts of Bobby Fischer memorabilia. It includes Fischer rarities such as his bible, his wristwatch and his wallet, a children’s book, an inscribed copy of his work, I was tortured in the Pasadena Jailhouse!, and five pocket chess sets. He also owns the publisher’s galley proofs of Fischer’s My 60 Memorable Games, along with the manuscript that originally only contained 52 games. Also in his collection is over a hundred Fischer scoresheets, among which is Bobby’s original game score, in his very distinctive hand, of the Game of the Century against Donald Byrne!

Also read: Sam Brady – Bobby Fischer's Game of the Century

About the author

John B. Henderson is a Scottish chess journalist, writer, and former daily chess columnist for The Scotsman, where he writes a long-running, near-daily chess column covering tournament news, historical anecdotes, and games. He is a long-time contributor to both Chess and New in Chess Magazines.

Though originally from Scotland (Glasgow), John has also lived and worked in Seattle, Washington. He holds a FIDE active rating (around 2132).

title: US Championships: So comes from behind to beat Robson, becomes sole leader
summary:
Wesley So defeated Ray Robson in round seven of the US Championship to take the sole lead on 5/7, half a point ahead of Fabiano Caruana and Andy Woodward. Awonder Liang suffered his second defeat, as he lost to Grigoriy Oparin. In the women's tournament, Alice Lee and Rachael Li share first place on 5½/7, followed closely by Irina Krush, while Thalia Cervantes suffered her first defeat of the event, against Anna Sargsyan. | Photo: Lennart Ootes / Saint Louis Chess Club

Open: A crucial victory for So

Wesley So emerged as the sole leader of the US Chess Championship after defeating Ray Robson with the black pieces in round seven. The three-time national champion now has 5/7 points, half a point ahead of Fabiano Caruana and Andy Woodward, who both drew their games. Awonder Liang, who had entered the round sharing first place, suffered his second defeat against Grigoriy Oparin and dropped to 4/7.

With four rounds remaining, So leads Caruana and Woodward by half a point. The eighth round will feature a direct encounter between So and Woodward, with the latter looking to catch the tournament leader before Sunday's rest day.

So's victory over Robson was far from straightforward. After obtaining a satisfactory position, he allowed his opponent to take control of the endgame. However, Robson failed to maintain his advantage as the players approached the first time control. Following inaccuracies by both sides, the position simplified into a bishop endgame in which So had two connected passed pawns. Robson was unable to find the precise defensive continuation, allowing So to secure his fourth victory of the tournament.

Robson v. So

Annotations by Martina Gerdts

In this position, White had to do something about the knight on d7, which he would actually have preferred to leave there. Since this was not possible without losing material, Robson chose 32.Nxf8 . In doing so, he exchanged the knight that he had just driven back to the last rank. 32.Nc5 does not work because Black takes on d7 and then wins a pawn on d4. 32.Nxb6 relieves the pressure on the d-pawn, allowing the other white knight to become active, while leaving Black with the knight on f8. For example, 32.Nxb6 cxb6 33.Bf4 Nc4 34.Nd2 would have been a playable line for White.

After 32.Nxf8 Rxf8 33.Nc5 Nc4 34.Bc3 , the timing was less favourable for the white bishop, leaving it more passive than in the alternative line.

35...Kg8 would have attacked the f-pawn without worsening the position of Black's knight. With 35...Nd6 , Wesley So made things easier for his opponent. 36.Nd7 would have prevented Black from also attacking the f-pawn with the rook. So was fortunate that 36.Re5 followed, allowing him to reply with 36...Kg8 .

The players transitioned into an endgame with same-coloured bishops, in which Wesley So had two connected extra pawns, while Robson's king was closer to the opposing pawns.

78.Kf5 would also have been better than 78.Kg6 , because the king would then not be standing behind the pawns that it is actually trying to stop.

Black is already winning after move 79 | Photo: Lennart Ootes

The most surprising result of the round was Oparin's victory over Liang. Playing white, Oparin obtained a promising position after his opponent made several questionable strategic decisions in the middlegame. Liang's pawn structure restricted the activity of his dark-squared bishop, leaving him with limited defensive resources. Further inaccuracies allowed Oparin to increase the pressure, and the game ended when Liang overlooked a direct mating threat.

Oparin v. Liang

Annotations by Martina Gerdts

In an already inferior position, Awonder Liang overlooked Grigoriy Oparin's mating threat and played 26...Bd8 . There followed 27.Bb7+ , and Black resigned.

Awonder Liang did not want to be shown the checkmate: 27...Kh8 28.Rxf8+ Ng6 29.Rxg8#.

Caruana and Woodward, meanwhile, were unable to keep pace with So. Caruana drew against Hans Niemann after a relatively balanced struggle, while Woodward split the point with Sam Sevian. The latter successfully defended against Woodward's attempts to generate attacking chances on the kingside.

The other decisive encounter saw Levon Aronian collect his first victory of the tournament by defeating Sam Shankland. Aronian made effective use of his bishop pair and successfully neutralised his opponent's counterplay.

Round 7 results

Standings after round 7

All games

Women's: Li and Lee both win, continue to share the lead

Alice Lee and Rachael Li scored victories in round seven of the US Women's Championship to keep the joint lead now on 5½/7 points. Lee defeated Rose Atwell, while Li got the better of Megan Paragua. A previous co-leader, Thalia Cervantes, suffered her first defeat against Anna Sargsyan and dropped out of first place. Eight-time national champion Irina Krush also won and now stands alone in third place on 5/7.

Lee recovered immediately from her sixth-round defeat against Li, which had ended a four-game winning streak. Playing black against Atwell, the 17-year-old initially faced some difficulties but gradually took control of the position. Atwell had opportunities to maintain the balance, but Lee eventually obtained the more promising prospects and converted her advantage.

Li, meanwhile, produced a convincing performance against Paragua. The 16-year-old employed an unusual opening setup before adopting an active approach in the middlegame. Her pieces became increasingly well coordinated, allowing her to generate threats that her opponent could not meet satisfactorily.

Li has now won five of her seven games, with her only defeat coming against Cervantes in round two.

Cervantes lost to Sargsyan after overextending her position. The former co-leader attempted to generate winning chances by opening lines on the kingside, but her plan backfired. Sargsyan exploited the resulting weaknesses, while Cervantes struggled to defend accurately under time pressure.

Krush also collected a full point, taking down defending champion Carissa Yip in a complicated encounter. The players reached a sharp position from a King's Indian Defence, with both sides obtaining opportunities. Under considerable time pressure, Yip eventually committed the decisive mistake, allowing Krush to secure her fourth victory of the championship.

title: European Club Cup - Live!

title: The European Club Cup kicks off in Budva
summary:
From 17 to 23 October, Budva in Montenegro will host the European Club Cup. With over 100 teams competing in the open section and 22 teams in the women's competition, it is a large-scale event. The favourites, in each of the sections, are teams from Türkiye and Monaco. The highest-rated players in the field are Nodirbek Abdusattorov, Wei Yi and Anish Giri. | Image: European Chess Union

The European Club Cup was originally due to take place in Herceg Novi. However, because work suddenly became necessary at Hotel Medun, which had been intended as the venue, the competition was moved at short notice to Budva, to a holiday resort on the Grdvica River.

The European Club Cup continues to grow. This year's edition already features 108 teams competing for the trophy in the open section, a few more than last year. The tournament is becoming increasingly popular, especially among amateurs, as with a little luck, they can face strong professional teams with their clubs or at least play close to the top players.

The tournament has the character of a Chess Olympiad, but anyone who wants to take part does not have to be a national-team player. The conditions set by the European Chess Union are fairly relaxed. Each federation may enter five teams, or four if no national championship is held within that federation. More teams may also be admitted on application. The federations themselves decide which of their clubs are eligible to participate.

Unlike the Chess Olympiad, the European Club Cup is played over six boards, making the tournament even more attractive to chess-loving amateurs because more players can take part.

Unlike in other sports, chess players may be registered and play simultaneously in several leagues. Professionals make extensive use of this feature. As a result, there is a kind of bidding competition among the stronger professional clubs for the best players. At the European Club Cup, they cannot play for all their clubs at the same time and therefore have to choose - usually the best financial offer.

The favourite teams

In previous years, strongly staffed teams from Russia were among the favourites, but times have changed. Russia has been suspended because of the war against neighbouring Ukraine and, as a consequence, has also left the European Chess Union and moved to Asia.

As a result, the Elo centre of gravity among the top teams has shifted elsewhere, geographically towards the south-west of the continent.

In the open section, the teams at the top of the starting list are more or less the same as last year. Defending champions Super Chess Romania have to do without Gukesh Dommaraju this year. The world champion has an important appointment coming up. Nodirbek Abdusattorov takes over the role of team leader on board one.

Ahead of Super Chess in the starting list are the Turkish Bayegan Pendik Chess Sports Club and the Macedonian team Alkaloid, both named after their sponsors. Alkaloid is a pharmaceutical company, while Bayegan operates in the petrochemical sector. Pendik is a district of Istanbul on the Asian side. The Turkish top club finished third in last year's final standings, while Alkaloid were second.

Bayegan Pendik Chess Sports Club have Anish Giri on board one and also include the two Turkish super-talents Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus and Ediz Gürel, as well as the young Russian Volodar Murzin, who competes under the FIDE flag. Amin Tabatabaei, Shakhriyar Mamedyarov and Richard Rapport add several more 2700 heavyweights to the fight for points.

Alkaloid counter with many players from India and China, led by Arjun Erigaisi and Wei Yi on the top boards.

Novy Bor are also always among the favourites, having already won the Cup three times. Last year, the Czech team had Vincent Keymer as one of their best scorers. He collected 5 points in 6 rounds. Novy Bor won bronze. Keymer is absent from this year's edition, however. Perhaps he has other things to do. Nihal Sarin and Pentala Harikrishna will lead the team.

Germany is represented by six clubs, but only two Bundesliga sides: Schachfreunde Berlin and St. Pauli, both of whom are competing without professionals. Also taking part are SC Erlangen, former Bundesliga club SV Mülheim-Nord, TSV Schönaich and SK Weiß Dame Hamburg.

With Vincent Keymer absent, Matthias Bluebaum is the highest-rated German player in the tournament. He plays on board two for the Hungarian team Tuxera Aquaprofit Nagykanizsai.

Women's Cup

The picture is somewhat easier to survey in the women's tournament, where matches are played over only four boards. As always, the clear favourites are the professional team Cercle d'échecs de Monte-Carlo. Monte-Carlo have already won the Women's Cup nine times, including last year, making them the record winners. Elisabeth Paehtz has been part of the team for many years and is playing for them again in Budva.

The teams Sirmium Sremska Mitrovica and Super Chess are the closest challengers for the tournament victory.

Two German clubs are also taking part: SG Löberitz and Klub Kölner Schachfreunde. Dana Reizniece-Ozola has played for Löberitz for many years. She was a minister in her native Latvia for a time and now works for FIDE. Reizniece-Ozola plays alongside four other Latvian players. Rebekka Schuster, vice-president of SG Löberitz, represents the German colours and presumably also serves as captain.

Klub Kölner Schachfreunde have entered an interesting lineup featuring streamers Katharina Reinicke and Hannah Sayce, Dutch player Anna Maia Kazarian and Poland's Anna Kantane.
